description: In 'phao lopia shelu theo' three nouns stand in a row, and nothing says where the reader ends and the thing read begins. Object 'ku' says it: the direct object starts at 'ku' and runs to the verb's own particles. It is optional and a clause without it is complete, so a speaker reaches for it when the edge or the role would otherwise be a guess. 'ko' (FOC) points at a word for contrast and leaves its role alone.
articulatory_notes: Raise the back of the tongue to the soft palate for voiceless 'k', release it, and round the lips closely for high back 'u'. As a single syllable it takes full stress.
usage_notes: 'ku' stands at the outer edge of the object phrase, before 'we' (ALSO) or 'li' (RESTR) and before any possessor. Everything between it and the Slot 1 particles, or the verb when there are none, is the object, so adjuncts stand before 'ku' and a manner word after it needs a Slot 1 particle in front. Before a clause's only phrase it marks an object whose subject is unsaid, and inside a relative clause it works the same way. In a causative the one made to act stands bare before it: 'phao lopia ku shelu ka theo'. A complement of 'nai' (be) or 'kelu' (become) is not an object and never takes it, and a passive clause has no object to mark.

examples.translation: The parent reads the child's book.
The parent's child reads the book.

examples.phi: lohau mua thepalu to nai. ku lopia to nila.
examples.translation: The dog was in the garden. It saw the child.

examples.phi: whu ku mia nila miona shua.
examples.translation: The person who sees me is coming.

pillars.peace-linguistics-practices: When an account of who acted on whom will be relied on, 'ku' lets the speaker fix the roles in the sentence itself instead of leaving them to a hearer's guess.
